patients.summary: Andre is a safety compliance officer who joins in 2018 with treated hepatitis B, hypertension, CKD attributed to heroin nephropathy, myeloma in remission after transplant, substance use disorders and a remote mitral repair. Over eight years he goes through nephrotic FSGS, adrenal Cushing syndrome and adrenalectomy, atrial fibrillation, a myeloma relapse with cast nephropathy, a cocaine-related inferior STEMI, a type A dissection repair and ARDS from pneumonia.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

34M establishing care, transferring from another primary care office in the area. Records requested, not here yet, so most of this is from him and his bottles.

He has a lot of history and gave it in a pretty matter-of-fact way:
- Hepatitis B, found in his twenties. Has been on tenofovir for years, started by a prior doctor. Admits he misses doses, maybe a couple of days a week.
- High blood pressure on amlodipine 5. Same story with adherence.
- Kidney disease. Told by his last office it was from heroin, never had a biopsy. Doesn't know his numbers.
- Multiple myeloma, diagnosed 2016 when he was 32. Had chemo and then a stem cell transplant at a cancer center in 2017. Says he's in remission and sees his oncologist every few months, next visit in November. No treatment now.
- Mitral valve repair, years ago, at an outside hospital. He isn't sure of the year.
- Substance use: injected heroin in his twenties, also used cocaine then. States he has not used for years. Opioid and cocaine use disorder carried on his old list.

Meds: tenofovir DF 300 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Social: works as a safety compliance officer, mostly at a desk, writes up inspections. Single, lives in South Hadley. Smokes about a pack a day, has for a long time. No alcohol at all. Not much exercise.

Family: father had a substance use problem and coronary disease in his early 50s (he thinks around 50). Mother has high blood pressure. Uncle on mom's side had multiple myeloma.

ROS: negative except as above. No chest pain, no swelling, no bone pain, no night sweats.

Exam: vitals as charted, BP 136/86. Well appearing. Pupils equal, no scleral icterus. Neck supple, no adenopathy. Heart regular, no murmur heard. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no hepatosplenomegaly. No edema. Skin clear.

A/P
1. CKD - attributed to heroin nephropathy. CMP and UA today, get old values from records.
2. HTN - a little above goal. Talked about taking the amlodipine every day before anything else.
3. Hep B on tenofovir - continue, refills sent. Will look for his last viral load in records.
4. Multiple myeloma in remission - followed by his oncologist, records requested.
5. Tobacco - smoking 1 ppd. Not ready to set a quit date. Brought it up, will keep at it.
6. Opioid/cocaine use disorder by history, IVDU - he reports none in years. Screening labs today: HIV, hep C.
7. Health maintenance: Tdap and flu shot today. Lipids and A1c.

Return in 3-4 months, sooner by text if needed.

documents.body: Tdap 0.5 mL IM right deltoid and influenza quadrivalent 0.5 mL IM left deltoid. VIS given for both. Screening questions negative, no prior vaccine reactions. Pt waited 15 min in lobby, left without issue.

Some protein in the urine. Blood counts, liver tests, sugar (A1c) and cholesterol are fine. HIV and hepatitis C tests are negative. Keep taking the tenofovir and amlodipine every day. Talk soon.

documents.author: hematology-oncology
documents.body:
TREATMENT SUMMARY - outside hematology-oncology

Patient: Andre Jackson, DOB 07/27/1984

Diagnosis: Kappa light-chain multiple myeloma, diagnosed June 2016.
Treatment: induction chemotherapy 2016-2017, followed by high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplant in 2017.
Current status: in remission, off therapy. Surveillance labs (serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, serum free light chains) every 4-6 months.
Other: chronic hepatitis B, continues tenofovir; please keep him on it.
Allergies: NKDA.

Next visit: November 2018.

documents.title: Hematology-Oncology Follow-up Letter
documents.author: hematology-oncology
documents.body:
Dear Doctor,

I saw Mr. Jackson today in follow-up for kappa light-chain myeloma, now about 18 months past autologous transplant. He feels well. No bone pain, no infections.

Today's SPEP shows no monoclonal protein and immunofixation is negative. Free light chain ratio is within the normal range. Counts are normal.

He remains in remission. We will see him again in 6 months with repeat studies. He is on tenofovir for his hepatitis B and I asked him to keep taking it daily.

Meds: tenofovir 300 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.

Thank you for letting us share his care.

Hematology-Oncology

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL EXAM

35 y/o M here for his yearly check. Feels well, nothing new to report.

PMH: chronic hep B on tenofovir; HTN; CKD 3b (attributed to heroin nephropathy); kappa light-chain myeloma in remission post ASCT 2017; opioid use disorder (heroin) and cocaine use disorder; s/p mitral valve repair.
Substance hx: IV use in his twenties. He tells me he has been clean for 8 years.

Meds: tenofovir DF 300 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily. Still misses doses of both here and there.
Allergies: none known.

Social: safety compliance officer, at a desk most of the day, gets very little exercise. Pack a day. No alcohol.
Family: as previously documented.

ROS negative.

Vitals normal today, BP 124/78.
Exam: NAD. HEENT normal. No nodes. Heart RRR. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abd soft, no organomegaly. No edema. Skin clear. Neuro grossly intact.
PHQ-2: 0.

A/P
1. Hep B - checking serologies today; haven't seen a panel since he joined.
2. HTN - at goal today.
3. CKD 3b - BMP.
4. Myeloma - in remission, oncology q6mo.
5. Tobacco - again advised to quit, he'll think about it.
6. HM: lipids, CBC. Flu shot done in the fall.

RTC 6 months.

documents.title: Hepatitis B Panel
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hep B panel: surface antigen negative, surface antibody positive, core antibody positive. So the surface antigen has cleared and he has antibody - the pattern of past infection, not active disease. Question is whether he still needs tenofovir. Will call his oncologist before changing anything given the myeloma/transplant history. Creatinine 2.4, slightly up. CBC and lipids unremarkable.

documents.title: Call With Hematology-Oncology
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Spoke with his hematologist-oncologist re: hep B panel (sAg neg, sAb pos, core Ab pos). Their recommendation: keep him on tenofovir indefinitely given myeloma history and the risk of reactivation if he ever needs treatment again. Agree. Called pt, explained the result and why we are not stopping the medicine. He was relieved, said he'd 'gotten used to it.' Encouraged daily dosing.

documents.title: Labs and kidney referral
documents.author: PCP

HIV and hepatitis C tests were negative again. The nephrology office has the referral; they'll call you, and if you don't hear by the end of next week let us know. Keep your feet up when you can and go easy on salt.

documents.title: Nephrology Consultation
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
NEPHROLOGY CONSULTATION

Referred by: primary care
Reason: edema, proteinuria, rising creatinine

Thank you for asking us to see Mr. Jackson, a 36-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B, hypertension, CKD previously attributed to heroin nephropathy, myeloma in remission and a prior mitral repair.

He describes swelling that began in his legs about four months ago and has spread up to his thighs and into the scrotum. He has gained about 9 kg (20 lb) over that time. His primary care office checked HIV and hepatitis C about six weeks ago; both were negative.

Substance use: when I asked directly he told me he has been injecting heroin daily for the last 8 years. Smokes a pack of cigarettes a day. No alcohol.

Meds: tenofovir DF 300 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, both taken irregularly.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father with substance use disorder; maternal uncle with multiple myeloma; mother with hypertension.

Exam: T 37.2 C, BP 148/102, P 98. Heart sounds distant; holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Breath sounds decreased at both bases. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness. 3+ pitting edema of both legs to the thighs; scrotum markedly edematous.

Labs today: BUN 34, creatinine 3.1, albumin 2.1, total cholesterol 305, ALT 32, AST 98. C3 low at 63, C4 22. HIV Ag/Ab negative. HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive. HCV antibody negative.
UA: protein 4+, RBC 40/hpf, WBC 10/hpf, leukocyte esterase 1+, occasional granular casts, no RBC casts.

Assessment:
1. Nephrotic syndrome with advanced CKD (now stage 4). With daily heroin injection the leading consideration is heroin-associated nephropathy (FSGS pattern), but he has never had tissue and he has a myeloma history, so I recommend a kidney biopsy.
2. Volume overload, marked.
3. Hypertension, above goal.

Plan:
- Start furosemide 40 mg daily. Low-salt diet.
- Percutaneous renal biopsy, scheduled 11/18.
- Labs 1 week after biopsy.
- Discussed his heroin use; he says he wants to cut down.

Nephrology

conditions.label: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis secondary to heroin use

reports.text:
Specimen: kidney, left, percutaneous needle core biopsy (2 cores).
Light microscopy: 21 glomeruli, several with segmental sclerosis of the tuft with adhesion to Bowman capsule. Tubules and interstitium without acute change. Arteries unremarkable. No casts, no crystals.
Immunofluorescence: no immune-complex deposition; nonspecific segmental IgM and C3 in sclerotic areas. Kappa and lambda stain evenly.
Electron microscopy: extensive podocyte foot process effacement. No electron-dense deposits.
reports.conclusion: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, consistent with heroin-associated nephropathy in this clinical setting. No evidence of light-chain disease.

documents.title: Renal Biopsy - Outside Record
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body: Ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy of the left kidney, 2 cores obtained with an 18-gauge needle. Tolerated well, no hematoma on post-procedure ultrasound. Observed 6 hours, discharged home. Pathology: FSGS, consistent with heroin-associated nephropathy; no light-chain deposition. Continue furosemide. Follow up in nephrology clinic.

documents.title: biopsy
documents.author: patient
documents.body: kidney dr said my biopsy was FSGS. what does that mean? also my legs are going down a lot with the water pill, peeing all morning

documents.title: RE: biopsy
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Hi Andre, FSGS means scarring in parts of the kidney filters, which is why protein is leaking. Your doctor will go over it in detail at your visit on 12/7. Good to hear the swelling is going down. Take the water pill in the morning so you aren't up at night.

He told nephrology he has been injecting heroin daily for the last 8 years. That is different from what he has told us. I asked him about it plainly today; he said he 'didn't want it in the chart here.' I'm going with the nephrology history as the accurate one. We talked about what the heroin is doing to his kidneys. He listened, was quiet, said he is trying to use less. I told him I'm not going anywhere and he can bring this up any time.

Swelling much better on furosemide. Weight 85 kg, down from 92 at nephrology. No dizziness. Still smoking a pack a day.

Exam: BP 142/90. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Trace ankle edema.

1. FSGS / nephrotic syndrome, CKD 4 - BMP today on furosemide. Nephrology follows.
2. Opioid use disorder, active IV heroin use - as above.

4. Hep B - tenofovir.

documents.title: Endocrinology Consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
ENDOCRINOLOGY CONSULTATION

Reason for referral: possible hypercortisolism.

Mr. Jackson is a 37-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B, hypertension, opioid and cocaine use disorders, FSGS from heroin-associated nephropathy (biopsy November 2020) with CKD stage 4, and multiple myeloma in remission. Over the past four months he has gained weight steadily, his proximal muscles have weakened, and he bruises easily. He takes no glucocorticoids in any form.

Meds: tenofovir DF 300 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
Social: safety compliance officer; smokes 1 ppd; no alcohol.
Family: father with substance use disorder; maternal uncle with myeloma; mother with hypertension.

Exam: BP 152/94. Rounded face. Fat pads above both clavicles.

Workup to date (drawn before this visit): plasma ACTH undetectable. Serum cortisol is elevated on morning and late-day samples. Overnight low-dose dexamethasone does not suppress his cortisol.

Impression: Cushing syndrome. With a suppressed ACTH the cortisol excess is ACTH-independent, which points to the adrenal gland rather than a pituitary or ectopic ACTH source.

Plan:
- High-dose dexamethasone suppression test given today, results to follow.
- Adrenal CT (without contrast given his kidney function) - ordered.
- Will see him back after imaging.

Endocrinology

reports.text:
TECHNIQUE: Axial non-contrast CT of the abdomen with thin sections through the adrenal glands.
COMPARISON: None.
FINDINGS: Left adrenal gland: well-circumscribed, smooth, homogeneous nodule measuring 3.4 cm, attenuation 8 HU. Right adrenal gland: normal. Liver, spleen and pancreas normal for a non-contrast study. Kidneys normal in size without hydronephrosis or calculi. No adenopathy. No ascites. Lung bases clear.
reports.conclusion: 3.4 cm left adrenal nodule with lipid-rich (8 HU) attenuation, consistent with adenoma. Normal right adrenal.

documents.title: CT Abdomen - Outside Report Received
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Outside CT abdomen report (11/17) received by fax and scanned. Routed to PCP.

documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up Letter
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Dear Doctor,

Mr. Jackson returned to review results.

The high-dose dexamethasone test did not suppress his cortisol. CT shows a 3.4 cm left adrenal nodule with attenuation of 8 HU and a normal right adrenal.

Diagnosis: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome due to a left adrenal adenoma.

I have referred him to endocrine surgery for laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. After surgery his remaining adrenal will be suppressed and he will need hydrocortisone for some months; we will manage the taper here. He understands and wants to go ahead.

Endocrinology

documents.title: surgery
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Surgery is jan 19 to take out the left adrenal. The surgeon said I'll be on steroids after. I thought steroids were the problem? Also can I keep taking my tenofovir and water pill before surgery

documents.title: RE: surgery
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good question. The tumor has been making too much cortisol, so your other adrenal gland has gone quiet. Once the tumor is out, your body won't make enough on its own for a while, so you take a small replacement dose (hydrocortisone) and come off it slowly as the other side wakes up. Very different from the high levels causing your symptoms now. The surgeon's team will tell you which pills to take the morning of surgery - generally keep the tenofovir going.

medications.sig: Take 3 tablets (15 mg) by mouth every morning and 1 tablet (5 mg) at 2 pm

reports.text:
Specimen: left adrenal gland, laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
Gross: adrenal gland with a well-circumscribed golden-yellow nodule, 3.4 cm in greatest dimension, confined to the gland. Margins grossly clear.
Microscopic: nodule composed of lipid-rich and compact cortical cells in nests and cords. No necrosis, no increased mitotic activity, no capsular or vascular invasion. Adjacent cortex thin.

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Endocrine Surgery
documents.author: endocrine surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Admitted: 01/19/2022  Discharged: 01/21/2022
Procedure: laparoscopic left adrenalectomy (01/19/2022)
Indication: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome from a 3.4 cm left adrenal adenoma.

Course: Uncomplicated laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. Given stress-dose hydrocortisone perioperatively, transitioned to oral replacement on POD 1. Ambulating, tolerating diet, pain controlled with acetaminophen. Creatinine at his baseline.

Pathology: benign adrenal cortical adenoma, 3.4 cm.

Discharge medications:
- NEW hydrocortisone 15 mg every morning and 5 mg at 2 pm
- tenofovir DF 300 mg daily
- amlodipine 5 mg daily
- furosemide 40 mg daily

Instructions: do not miss hydrocortisone doses. Sick-day rules reviewed - double the dose for fever and call if vomiting. Endocrinology will manage the taper.
Allergies: NKDA.

Endocrine Surgery

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD

CC: chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations

HPI: 38-year-old man who was leading a safety briefing at his job about an hour before arrival when he abruptly felt his heart racing, chest discomfort and shortness of breath. Reports a lot of stress at work lately. History of adrenal Cushing syndrome treated with adrenalectomy, CKD stage 4 from FSGS, hepatitis B, hypertension, myeloma in remission, remote mitral valve repair. No arrhythmia or coronary disease in the past.

Meds: tenofovir, amlodipine, furosemide. NKDA.
Family hx: father had coronary artery disease at 50.
Social: 1 ppd smoker.

Exam: BP 150/95, HR 120 irregular, RR 22, SpO2 97% on room air. Anxious but nontoxic. Lungs clear to auscultation. Heart irregularly irregular, tachycardic. No leg edema.

Data: troponin I <0.04 ng/mL. BNP 80 pg/mL. TSH 2.5. CBC within normal limits. Creatinine near his known baseline.
ECG: atrial fibrillation with RVR, no acute ST changes.

ED course: diltiazem 10 mg IV x1 then infusion. Converted spontaneously to sinus rhythm at about 15:15; repeat ECG sinus 78. Symptoms resolved. Repeat vitals BP 134/84, HR 78.

Assessment: new-onset paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with RVR, converted. CHA2DS2-VASc 1 (hypertension). Discussed anticoagulation: not starting at this score.

Disposition: discharged home. Start metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily. Follow up with PCP this week; cardiology referral recommended.

Emergency Medicine

reports.text:
Specimen: kidney, percutaneous needle core biopsy.
Light microscopy: glomeruli show diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane. Many distal tubules contain dense, fractured, angulated casts with a surrounding cellular reaction.
Immunofluorescence: tubular casts stain for kappa light chain with minimal lambda (kappa-restricted).
Electron microscopy: subepithelial electron-dense deposits along the glomerular basement membrane.
reports.conclusion: Light-chain (myeloma) cast nephropathy, kappa-restricted. Glomerular basement membrane thickening with subepithelial deposits; correlate with hepatitis B status.

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Medicine
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Admitted: 11/05/2023  Discharged: 11/14/2023

Principal diagnosis: relapsed kappa light-chain multiple myeloma with cast nephropathy.
Other: nephrotic syndrome; acute on chronic kidney injury (CKD 4); hepatitis B reactivation; FSGS (biopsy 2020); hypertension; paroxysmal AF; s/p mitral valve repair; s/p left adrenalectomy.

Hospital course:
Admitted from the ED with three weeks of edema and frothy urine, creatinine 4.6 and nephrotic-range proteinuria. Hepatitis B surface antigen, negative in 2020, is now positive with mildly raised transaminases (ALT 78, AST 64). Serum free kappa light chain 1,860 mg/L, kappa/lambda ratio 155.

Kidney biopsy 11/8: kappa-restricted light-chain cast nephropathy, plus GBM thickening with subepithelial deposits.

Hematology-oncology started daratumumab, bortezomib and dexamethasone on 11/9, first cycle given inpatient, with acyclovir prophylaxis. Tenofovir continued; adherence discussed at length - he must not miss doses during treatment.

Furosemide continued for edema. Creatinine 4.1 at discharge. No dialysis needed.

Discharge medications:
- NEW acyclovir 400 mg twice daily
- NEW dexamethasone 20 mg on the day of and the day after each bortezomib dose (per oncology calendar)
- Daratumumab and bortezomib at the oncology clinic per cycle schedule
- tenofovir DF 300 mg daily - TAKE EVERY DAY
- amlodipine 5 mg daily
- metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily
- furosemide 40 mg daily

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week; hematology-oncology 11/16 for cycle 1 continuation; nephrology 2 weeks.
Allergies: NKDA.

Hospital Medicine

What happened: swelling came back, creatinine 4.6, biopsy showed myeloma cast nephropathy - his myeloma is back. Hep B surface antigen positive again. Started daratumumab/bortezomib/dex on 11/9 with acyclovir.

He's shaken. Says the November oncology visit was going to be 'routine.' Sleeping poorly on dex days. Taking tenofovir every day now - showed me the pill box. Swelling down some.

Meds reconciled: acyclovir 400 BID, dex 20 mg per cycle days, dara/bortezomib at clinic, tenofovir DF 300, amlodipine 5, metoprolol succinate 25, furosemide 40.

Exam: BP 134/84. Tired appearing. Heart regular. Lungs clear. 1-2+ edema to mid shin.

A/P
1. Relapsed myeloma with cast nephropathy - oncology driving; BMP and CBC today to see where we are.
2. AKI on CKD 4 - creatinine 4.1 at discharge, nephrology f/u booked.
3. Hep B reactivation - tenofovir, daily. Oncology following LFTs.
4. Dex insomnia - take it in the morning.
5. Cancel 11/29 visit (seen today), RTC 6-8 weeks.

Diagnosis: inferior STEMI, cocaine-associated. Single-vessel CAD.

Counseling: cocaine caused this heart attack and can cause another; strongly advised to stop. Smoking cessation advised.

- NEW aspirin 81 mg daily

ED NOTE

41M with cocaine use disorder and an inferior STEMI last year, now with abrupt, severe, sharp chest pain he calls 'tearing,' going straight through to his back. Used cocaine earlier today.

BP 180/110, HR 105, RR 22. Diaphoretic, in obvious distress. Breath sounds diminished on the left. Extremities cool, capillary refill delayed.

Portable CXR: widened mediastinum, small left effusion. Bedside echo: intimal flap in the ascending aorta.
CTA chest: type A dissection.

IV esmolol and nicardipine started. Cardiac surgery at bedside; to OR emergently. Ticagrelor last dose this morning - surgery and blood bank aware.

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Cardiac Surgery
documents.author: cardiac surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Admitted 10/30/2025, discharged 11/12/2025

Diagnosis: acute Stanford type A aortic dissection, cocaine-associated.
Procedure 10/30/2025: emergent replacement of the ascending aorta with hemiarch repair under circulatory arrest; redo sternotomy (prior mitral repair).

Course: Taken to the OR from the ED. Platelet transfusion for recent ticagrelor. Extubated POD 1. ICU 4 days. Creatinine rose after surgery and settled near 3.8; no dialysis. Mitral repair inspected intraoperatively, intact. No atrial fibrillation during the stay. Ticagrelor stopped - he was within days of finishing 12 months of DAPT; aspirin continues. Metoprolol increased for strict blood pressure and heart rate control.

Discharge medications:
- CHANGED metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily
- STOPPED ticagrelor
- aspirin 81 mg daily
- atorvastatin 80 mg nightly
- amlodipine 5 mg daily
- furosemide 40 mg daily
- nitroglycerin SL prn
- tenofovir DF 300 mg daily
- acyclovir 400 mg twice daily
- daratumumab: oncology to decide when to resume
- acetaminophen as needed for incision pain

Target BP under 120/80. No lifting over 10 lb for 8 weeks. No cocaine - another dissection or heart attack could be fatal.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week, cardiac surgery 4 weeks, cardiology.
Allergies: NKDA.

documents.title: ICU Admission Note
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
MICU ADMISSION NOTE

41-year-old man, two months out from repair of a type A aortic dissection, with chronic hepatitis B, relapsed kappa light-chain myeloma on daratumumab maintenance (on hold since the surgery), CKD stage 4, prior mitral valve repair, CAD with RCA stent. Several days of feeling feverish at home, worsening breathlessness - worse when he lies flat - and a cough bringing up yellow sputum.

Meds: metoprolol succinate 100, aspirin 81, atorvastatin 80, amlodipine 5, furosemide 40, tenofovir DF 300, acyclovir 400 BID. NKDA.
Social: 1 ppd smoker, no alcohol, safety compliance officer.
Family: father SUD, mother HTN, maternal uncle myeloma.

On arrival: RR 28, T 38.9 C, SpO2 88% on room air. Bilateral crackles.
ABG on room air: pH 7.48 / PaCO2 30 / PaO2 58 / HCO3 24.
WBC 18,000 with a left shift.
CXR: bilateral alveolar infiltrates.

Course so far: IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin, cefepime - renally dosed) started in the ED. Despite this his breathing got worse and he was intubated. Ventilated at 6 mL/kg predicted body weight; peak pressures high, oxygenation remains poor on FiO2 0.8.

Assessment: acute hypoxemic respiratory failure - ARDS from community-acquired pneumonia in an immunocompromised host, with refractory hypoxemia.
Plan: lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning, neuromuscular blockade, conservative fluids once perfused, cultures pending, continue antibiotics.

Critical Care

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Pulmonary and Critical Care
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Admitted 12/31/2025 - Discharged 01/20/2026

Diagnoses: ARDS with refractory hypoxemia due to community-acquired pneumonia. Organism not identified.

Course: Intubated on the day of admission for worsening hypoxemia despite antibiotics and fluids. Lung-protective ventilation with high peak pressures and poor oxygenation on FiO2 0.8. Proned for four sessions with neuromuscular blockade for 48 hours; oxygenation improved steadily afterward. Vancomycin and cefepime, renally dosed, for 7 days. Blood cultures no growth; sputum culture normal respiratory flora. Extubated 01/09/2026. Transferred to the floor 01/12. Worked with physical therapy - deconditioned but walking with a walker at discharge, then without by the last day. Creatinine 3.8, near his baseline. No arrhythmia. Daratumumab remains on hold; oncology will decide timing.

Discharge medications (unchanged from admission): metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 80 mg nightly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, nitroglycerin SL prn, tenofovir DF 300 mg daily, acyclovir 400 mg twice daily.

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week; pulmonary clinic 6 weeks with chest X-ray; oncology.
Smoking: advised to quit. Allergies: NKDA.

Pulmonary & Critical Care

reports.text: PA and lateral chest. Interval clearing of the previously seen bilateral alveolar opacities. No new consolidation. No pleural effusion. Sternotomy wires and postoperative aortic changes.
reports.conclusion: Clearing of the bilateral opacities since the 12/31/2025 study.

documents.title: Pulmonary Clinic Letter
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
Dear Doctor,

I saw Mr. Jackson about six weeks after discharge from the MICU for ARDS due to community-acquired pneumonia.

He is walking a mile now and climbs his stairs without stopping. Minimal cough. Still smoking.

Oxygen saturation on room air normal at rest. Lungs clear.

Chest X-ray today shows clearing of the bilateral opacities.

Assessment: recovering well from ARDS. Smoking cessation is the most important thing he can do for his lungs; we discussed this again. No routine pulmonary follow-up needed; happy to see him if symptoms return.

Pulmonology

documents.title: Hematology-Oncology Follow-up Letter
documents.author: hematology-oncology
documents.body:
Dear Doctor,

Mr. Jackson returns after a long interruption in daratumumab: held since his aortic dissection repair in October and through his ICU admission for pneumonia and ARDS. He has recovered well.

Myeloma remains in very good partial response off therapy for these months. We resumed daratumumab every 4 weeks today. Continue acyclovir and tenofovir.
